name: LM2733YMFX_NOPB
title: Current-mode boost converter, 40 V internal FET, 1.6 MHz (X) or 0.6 MHz (Y), SOT-23

source.revision: SNVS209G, November 2002, revised May 2019 (addendum pages dated 2025)

summary: The LM2733 is a step-up switching regulator in a five-pin SOT-23 with a 40 V DMOS switch on chip, run at a fixed frequency under peak-current-mode control with the loop compensated inside. Two frequency options exist: X switches at 1.6 MHz and Y at 600 kHz. It works from 2.7 V to 14 V, limits the switch current cycle by cycle at 1 A minimum (duty cycle up to 50 %), and has thermal shutdown. Pulling SHDN low turns it off, drawing under 1 µA.

circuits.title: 5 V to 12 V boost, X version (typical application)
circuits.description: Steps 5 V up to 12 V with the 1.6 MHz part, rated for about 330 mA of load. The inductor L1 runs from the input to SW; while the internal FET is on it charges, and when the FET turns off its current flows through the Schottky D1 into the output capacitor C2. The divider R1 over R2 feeds FB, which regulates at 1.23 V, and CF across R1 places the loop zero the converter needs to be stable. R3 pulls SHDN up to the input so the part runs until SHDN is driven low. C1 is the ceramic input reservoir.
notes: The low-voltage column of Table 1 (Figure 24) is this circuit with R3 = 47 kΩ in place of 51 kΩ.

operation.text: Each clock cycle an S-R latch turns the FET on. A 50 mΩ resistor in series with the FET turns its current into a voltage, which is added to a ramp from the ramp generator and fed to the PWM comparator. The other comparator input is the output of a Gm error amplifier driven from FB, so when the sensed signal reaches it the latch resets and the FET turns off. In this way the feedback sets the peak FET current each cycle to hold the output in regulation.

Q1 and Q2 with R3 to R6 form the bandgap reference. The loop drives the output until the two transistors carry equal currents, so the output settles at the FB voltage scaled up by the ratio of the external divider.

A current limit comparator watches the same sense voltage and drives the latch directly: once the FET current reaches the threshold the FET switches off and stays off until the next clock pulse, whatever the PWM comparator is doing. The limit is at least 1 A for duty cycles up to 50 % and falls at higher duty cycles (Figures 26 and 27).
A thermal shutdown block resets the latch and so turns the switch off when the die overheats.

Inside: VIN (pin 5) feeds the reference made of Q1, Q2 (marked ×10 against Q1), R3 30k, R4 140k, R5 and R6, with FB (pin 3) on the base of Q1. The Gm amplifier output, loaded by RC and CC to ground, goes to the PWM comparator, whose other input is the sum of the ramp generator and the amplified current-sense signal. The PWM comparator, the current limit comparator and thermal shutdown each reset the flip-flop, which the oscillator sets; its output drives the FET gate through a driver. The FET drain is SW (pin 1) and its 0.05 Ω sense resistor returns to GND (pin 2). SHDN (pin 4) feeds the shutdown circuitry.

Typical switching frequency is 1.6 MHz for the X version, 600 kHz for Y. The higher frequency allows smaller, cheaper inductors and capacitors for a given output, at the cost of slightly lower efficiency, since each cycle's fixed switching loss is paid more often, and typically worse EMI, which lands higher in the spectrum where circuits are more sensitive. The Y version needs more minimum inductance because its period is longer.

Pulling SHDN low turns the part off; above 1.5 V it runs and below 0.50 V it is off, drawing 0.024 µA typical and 1 µA at most. The pin must never be left open. Without the shutdown function, connect it to VIN; a 47 kΩ resistor between the two pins is recommended in that case. With the shutdown function, pull it up to VIN through roughly 50 kΩ to 100 kΩ. Its voltage must not exceed VIN.
The input range is 2.7 V to 14 V.

Multilayer ceramic capacitors suit the part best for their low ESR and high resonant frequency. Use only X5R or X7R dielectrics; Z5U and Y5F parts can lose so much capacitance over temperature and bias that as little as 20 % of the rating remains. Taiyo-Yuden, AVX and Murata are named as sources.

One ceramic capacitor of 4.7 µF to 10 µF is enough for most designs; for outputs under 10 V use 10 µF. Tantalum capacitors can be added in parallel for line support and transient response. Ultra-low-ESR aluminium types such as Sanyo Oscon work but are costly; ordinary aluminium electrolytics do not suit switching above 500 kHz because of ringing and self-heating from ripple current. Too much output ESR can erode phase margin and make the loop unstable.

The input capacitor supplies the current pulse drawn into the inductor each time the switch turns on, so it must have very low ESR: ceramic, 2.2 µF nominal, larger allowed. It also reduces the ripple at VIN and the EMI conducted back up the supply line.
Despite the internal compensation, Cf across R1 is required for stability: it adds a zero to the loop response and without it the loop can oscillate. Put the zero at about 8 kHz.

Use a Schottky diode. Switch voltage under 15 V: a 20 V part such as MBR0520; 15 V to 25 V: a 30 V part such as MBR0530; over 25 V: a 40 V part such as MBR0540. The MBR05xx parts handle 0.5 A average; between 0.5 A and 1 A average a Microsemi UPS5817 can be used.
R1 from the output to FB and R2 from FB to ground set VOUT. R2 of about 13.3 kΩ is recommended, which puts about 92 µA through the divider; R1 then follows from the divider equation.

The maximum duty cycle limits the highest output-to-input ratio reachable in continuous mode. Losses in the inductor windings, switching and capacitor ripple heating make the real duty cycle slightly higher than the ideal formula; 1 - efficiency × VIN / VOUT is a good estimate.

operation.topic: Inductor size and ripple, worked example
operation.text: A larger inductor gives less ripple current and so usually less output ripple, and since the peak current is fixed by the limit it raises the load power available; too small an inductor can cap the load current. Continuous operation at the loads of interest usually gives the best load regulation and lowest ripple, and every boost converter becomes discontinuous at light enough load. Example, X version, 5 V to 12 V with 10 µH, assuming VDIODE = 0.5 V and VSW = 0.5 V: the period is about 0.625 µs, the duty cycle 62.5 %, the on-time 0.390 µs and the off-time 0.235 µs. About 4.5 V sits across the inductor while the switch is on, so its current rises at 0.45 A/µs, ramping up 0.176 A in the on-time and down by as much in the off-time; the average inductor current is ILOAD / (1 - DC). Below about 33 mA of load the current reaches zero and the converter goes discontinuous.

VSW in the equations depends on load current and is about the FET on-resistance times the average inductor current. On-resistance rises at VIN below 5 V because the gate gets less drive; above VIN = 5 V the gate voltage is clamped internally at 5 V (Figure 10). The peak switch current is guaranteed above 1 A below 50 % duty cycle; at higher duty cycles see Figures 26 and 27.

At high duty cycles the longer on-time means dissipation in the FET, rather than the current limit, sets the maximum output current. Its conduction loss is DC × IIND(AVE)² × RDSON, and the switching losses on top call for some derating. RθJA is 210 °C/W in the SOT-23 package.

Where the load is small the inductor may be made as small as possible and the converter run discontinuously, provided the switch current never reaches the 1 A limit within one on-time. Example: X version at its 1.15 MHz minimum frequency, 5 V in, 12 V out, a 0.3 V diode drop and 0.2 V across the switch. The period is at most 0.870 µs, the duty cycle 60.3 %, the longest on-time 0.524 µs (off-time 0.346 µs) and 4.8 V is across the inductor, giving a minimum of 2.5 µH. A 2.7 µH part would do if it holds that inductance up to 1 A.

Pick an inductor whose continuous current rating keeps it out of saturation at the peak currents, with a core type of low core (switching) loss, and allow for winding loss in the current rating. Sumida, Coilcraft, Panasonic, TDK and Murata are named as suppliers.
The maximum load current equation gives a calculated figure; Figures 28 and 29 give the maximum load current measured on a typical device for 15 V to 40 V outputs against input voltage.

Place every part as close to the LM2733 as possible; a four-layer board with internal ground planes is recommended. Keep the L1, D1, C2 loop very short, since trace inductance in series with D1 and C2 adds noise and ringing. Keep R1, R2 and CF near the FB pin so noise is not picked up on that trace. With an internal ground plane, take pin 2 of U1 and the negative ends of C1 and C2 straight to it with vias.

The suggested placement puts U1 in the middle with C1 beside it and L1 to the right over the VIN copper; D1 and C2 sit above U1 with D1 running to the VOUT copper; R1, CF and R2 stand down the left side next to U1, R3 below it on the shutdown trace, and ground vias sit at C2, C1 and between the top pads of U1 beside pin 1.
The built-in ESD protection is limited: store and handle the part with its leads shorted or in conductive foam so the MOS gates are not damaged.
